items.text: This Directive applies to natural persons who are suspects or accused persons in criminal proceedings. It applies at all stages of the criminal proceedings, from the moment when a person is suspected or accused of having committed a criminal offence, or an alleged criminal offence, until the decision on the final determination of whether that person has committed the criminal offence concerned has become definitive.

provisions.textEn:
(1) The status of defendant (arguido) is assigned to any person who has been accused (at the end of the phase of inquiry) or against whom the optional phase of instruction (which consists of a judicial appraisal of the decision taken at the end of the inquiry) has been requested.

(2) The status of defendant remains valid during all stages of the criminal procedure.

(3) The provisions of Article 58, paragraphs (2) to (6), shall apply as appropriate.

For the purposes of this Code (…), a 'suspect' is any person regarding whom there is sign that he/she has committed or is preparing to commit an offence, or has participated or is preparing to participate in an offence.

(1) If, during the course of an interrogation of a person who is not a defendant, a founded suspicion emerges that this person has committed an offence, the authority carrying out the interrogation shall suspend it immediately and effect the communication and the advice mentioned in Article 58 (2) CCP.

(2) A person suspected of having committed an offence has the right to be designated as a defendant at his/her own request, whenever an investigation is being carried out with a view to establishing his/her criminal liability and measures are being taken which personally affect him/her.

(3) The provisions of article 58 (3) and (4) apply as appropriate.

provisions.comment: See the comment to this provision in Article 2 of the Directive 2013/48.
provisions.textEn:
(1) Without detriment to Article 57, the designation as defendant (arguido) is also mandatory as soon as:

(a) A person makes statements before any judicial authority or criminal police body during an inquiry initiated against him/her, where there are grounds to suspect that such person has committed a criminal offence;

(b) A coercive or patrimonial guarantee measure must be imposed on him/her;

(c) A suspect is arrested under the terms and for the purposes of Articles 254 to 261 of this Code; or

(d) A police report has been drawn up identifying a person as an alleged offender and that person has been informed on the contents thereof, unless the report is clearly unfounded.

(2) The status of defendant is acquired with the communication to the concerned person, either orally or in writing, by a judicial authority or criminal police body that, as of that moment, he/she has the status of defendant in criminal proceedings and, if necessary, by the explanation of procedural rights and duties of defendants laid down in Article 61, which he/she is thenceforth bound to observe.

(3) If the act is carried out by the criminal police, it must be communicated to a judicial authority within 10 days, so that this authority may, within another 10-day term, examine and decide whether or not the act is to be considered valid.

(4) The status of arguido implies the delivery to the concerned person, if possible simultaneously, of a document specifying details on the case and on the defence attorney, if one has already been appointed, and such a document must also indicate the rights and duties that the person is thenceforth entitled to.

(5) Failure to comply with the formalities laid down in this Article carry a prohibition to use as evidence any statements made by the concerned person.

(6) The non-validation of the act designating a person as arguido by the judicial authority does not affect the evidence that has been previously collected.

items.comment:
I - In order to understand properly Portuguese criminal procedure, it is essential to be acquainted with the concept of arguido, since this is a nuclear and somewhat distinctive concept of Portuguese criminal procedure:

- The suspect of a crime, as such, does not have any formal status in Portuguese criminal procedure, meaning that he/she does not have any special procedural right or duty. Only the formal designation of a person as a subject of the procedure (an ‘arguido’) gives rise to such rights and duties. Thus, this procedural act is extremely important for the person concerned, which is why the moment and the conditions of such act are regulated in detail in the CCP.

- Authorities designate a person as arguido in the cases where this is imposed by law, namely when there is an inquiry where a certain person is suspected of having committed a crime and he/she makes a statement before the judicial authority or the police. Moreover, any person may request to be designated as arguido if he/she is suspected of having committed a crime and measures are being carried out which personally affect him/her. When designating someone as an arguido, authorities must inform the person about the rights which spring up from this procedural role, and, if necessary, explain such rights to him/her (if the person has already been designated as arguido when he/she is questioned, he/she must be informed of these rights again and, if necessary, given proper elucidation: Articles 61 (1) (h), 141 (4), 143 (2) and 144 (1) of the CCP.). The status of arguido remains in place until the end of the criminal procedure.

- In addition to the rights which everyone is entitled to vis-à-vis the State, and the rights which other formal subjects of the criminal procedure are also entitled to, a person who has been designated as an arguido is specifically entitled to a set of rights which, together, form one fundamental 'right of defence', guaranteed by Article 61 (1) of the CPP, some of which have constitutional rank. An arguido is entitled to the following rights: (a) to be present in all procedural acts of direct concern to him/her; (b) to be heard; (c) to be informed of the acts which are imputed to him/her; (d) to remain silent; (e) to appoint a lawyer or request that one be appointed to him/her; (f) to be assisted by a defence lawyer in every procedural act in which he/she takes part, and, if arrested, to communicate with him/her in private; (g) to intervene in the investigation phases of the procedure, e.g. by providing evidence or requesting that investigative measures be conducted; (h) to be informed of the rights springing from this status; (i) if he/she is a minor (under 18 years old), to be accompanied in any procedural act that he/she is to attend by the persons who exercise parental responsibilities over him/her, by his/her legal representative or a person who holds his/her factual guardianship, or yet, if the former cannot be reached or special circumstances concerning his/her best interest so require, by another adequate person indicated by him/her and agreed to by the judicial authority; and (j) to appeal the decisions that personally affect him/her.

- Conversely, an arguido is bound to certain specific duties which are set out in Article 61 (3) of the CCP, namely the following: (a) to be present before a judge, a public prosecutor or a police officer, where imposed by law and upon being regularly convened to do so; (b) to be truthful on his/her identity; (c) to be subjected to investigative measures aimed at gathering evidence, and to coercive measures and patrimonial warrants aimed, inter alia, at securing his/her presence at trial; and (d) to be subjected to a peculiar coercive measure named ‘statement of identity and residence’ (termo de identidade e residência), which involves a duty not to change residence and not to absent oneself for more than five days without notifying the authorities, failure to comply with which may legitimise a trial in absentia.


II - On the other hand, it also seems convenient to outline the pre-trial or investigative phases of Portuguese criminal procedure:

- In Portugal a standard criminal procedure has two pre-trial phases: (i) inquiry (inquérito: Articles 262 f. CCP), and (ii) instruction (instrução: Articles 286 f. CCP). The former is the phase where the crime is subject to an investigation in a stricter sense of the term, and it ends with a decision (normally by the public prosecution) as to whether or not the person should be prosecuted, which depends on whether or not there is a stronger probability of this person being guilty and convicted than innocent and acquitted. The latter is an assessment, by a judge, of the decision taken at the end of the inquiry. The phase of instruction is optional, as it will only take place if it is requested by certain procedural subjects, notably the arguido, and it comprises any measures deemed important by the judge (which may include further investigative measures), as well as a mandatory oral debate with the participation of the public prosecution and the arguido (and possibly other subjects such as the victim). After the debate, the judge decides whether or not the arguido is to stand trial (indicted).


III - In view of the above information, it is safe to conclude that the concepts of 'suspect' and 'accused' persons used in the Directive are fully accommodated in the concept of 'arguido' used in the Portuguese legal system, since: (i) on the one hand, a person who is accused or indicted is necessarily designated as an arguido; and, (ii) on the other hand, this procedural status must also be assigned to a person regarding which there is founded suspicion of having committed the crime being investigated.

items.heading: CHAPTER 2

items.text: Member States shall ensure that suspects and accused persons are presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law.
items.heading: Article 3

provisions.comment: A sentence becomes definitive when it is no longer open to ordinary appeal. Nevertheless, it may still be appealed from through an extraordinary or exceptional form of appeal, namely: (1) Appeals aimed at settling conflicting jurisprudence: should there be two opposite decisions proffered by high courts, by a high court and the Supreme Court, or by the Supreme Court itself, in different cases, concerning the same legal issue, then the Supreme Court may be called upon to solve the contradiction by adopting one of the conflicting approaches (see Articles 437 f. CCP). (2) Appeals of review: pursuant to Articles 449 f. CCP, this type of appeal is possible if: (a) another definitive decision established as false evidence which had been central to the conviction; (b) another definitive decision deemed proven that a judge or lay-judge committed a crime connected to their function in the procedure; (c) the facts upon which the conviction was based are so irreconcilable with facts that have been proven in another sentence as to raise strong doubts on the fairness of the conviction; (d) new facts or evidence are discovered that raise strong doubts on the fairness of the conviction (however, appeals on this ground are not admissible for the sole purpose of reviewing the quantum of penalty concretely applied); or (e) it is discovered that evidence which had been crucial to the conviction was obtained through prohibited methods. Prohibited methods for gathering evidence are described in Article 126 (1) to (3) CCP. According to the first of those provisions, evidence obtained through torture, coercion or, in general, through physical or psychological harm to a person is null and cannot be used. This configures an absolute nullity. Article 126 (2) specifies that a method is deemed to be “harmful” when it involved: (a) intervention into the free-will of the concerned person through maltreatment, physical harm, administration of means of any nature, hypnosis or use of cruel or deceptive means; (b) perturbation, by any means, of the capacity of memory or of understanding of the person; (c) use of force beyond the cases and limits admitted by the law; (d) threatening the individual with the execution of a legally inadmissible measure or with the denegation or conditioning of a legally guaranteed benefit; or (e) promising a legally inadmissible benefit. In turn, Article 126 (3) establishes that, to the exception of the cases where the law provides otherwise, evidence obtained through intrusion, without the consent of the person concerned, in his/her private life, domicile, mail or telecommunications is also null. One difference vis-à-vis the former methods is that, in these cases, the person concerned may consent to the intrusion, either ex ante or ex post facto, and, if so, the nullity will be cured – thus, this constitutes a (merely) relative nullity. Moreover, whereas the nullity established by Articles 126 (1) and (2) bears no exceptions, Article 126 (3), as noted, excepts the cases “where the law provides otherwise", which is a reference to the intrusive investigative measures allowed for in the CCP (Articles 171 f.) and in other special legal instruments of criminal procedure.
provisions.textEn: Every defendant is presumed innocent until a sentence convicting him/her has become definitive, and must be tried as swiftly as compatible with defence guarantees.

The law may only restrict rights, freedoms and guarantees in cases expressly provided for in the Constitution, and such restrictions must not exceed that which is necessary for safeguarding other rights and interests protected by the Constitution.

provisions.comment: This provision is particularly important concerning evidentiary issues, and therefore it is addressed to a further extent below, as a comment to Article 6 (1) of the Directive.
provisions.textEn: Criminal procedure has accusatorial structure, and the trial hearing and the indictment-related acts required by law subject to the principle audi alteram partem [princípio do contraditório].

items.heading: Article 4
items.comment: Only partially implemented, as expounded below, notably in the comment to Article 18 (1) of the Constitution.

items.text: 1. Member States shall take the necessary measures to ensure that, for as long as a suspect or an accused person has not been proved guilty according to law, public statements made by public authorities, and judicial decisions, other than those on guilt, do not refer to that person as being guilty. This shall be without prejudice to acts of the prosecution which aim to prove the guilt of the suspect or accused person, and to preliminary decisions of a procedural nature, which are taken by judicial or other competent authorities and which are based on suspicion or incriminating evidence.

provisions.comment:
The right to be presumed innocent constitutes a fundamental principle of Portuguese criminal procedure and it is enshrined in the Constitution (in the aforementioned Article 32 (2)) within the category of 'rights, freedoms and guarantees' (direitos, liberdades e garantias).

Pursuant to Article 18 (1) of the Constitution, this entails that this principle is directly applicable and binding all public and private entities. “Direct applicability”, in this context, means that those rights, freedoms and guarantees (which include presumption of innocence) apply even in the absence of any concretisation in the law, and prevail over conflicting legal norms. “Binding” means that any public or private entity is obliged to respect those rights, freedoms and guarantees even if no particular legal norm provides for specific obligations. The consequences of the principle of presumption of innocence are therefore not limited to a specific or, even, to an ascertainable set of procedural moments, but rather they are no less than transversal to the procedural system (including the organisation and functioning of the courts and rules on remand). Ultimately, it is the presumption of innocence that explains the wide array of defence rights which is attributed to a defendant. Article 18 (1) of the Constitution is key for assessing the implementation of this Directive into the Portuguese legal system, because sometimes it is the only (or, at least, the main) normative basis accommodating the provisions of the Directive.

That is precisely the case with Article 4 (1). Indeed, apart from Article 343 (2) CCP – which provides that, at the trial hearing, the court shall hear the defendant “without expressing any opinion or making any comment that allow for inferring a judgement on his/her guilt” –, no provision in the law clearly prohibits authorities from issuing public statements referring to a defendant as being guilty, or requires specific measures to be carried out with a view to avoiding or sanctioning such an action. It is true that several legal provisions establish a general duty on judges, prosecutors and different police bodies not to make public statements or comments concerning criminal proceedings in which they intervene (see Article 12 (1) of Law no. 21/85 (on judges), Article 84 (1) of Law no. 47/86 (on public prosecutors), Article 13 (2) of Law no. 37/2008 (on the Judiciary Police), Article 12 of Decree-Law no. 297/2009 (on the National Republican Guard), and Article 14 (1) and (2) of Decree-Law no. 243/2015 (on the Public Security Police)). There are also substantive and procedural provisions aimed at preventing public disclosure of information concerning ongoing investigations (see, notably, Articles 86 f. CCP, and Article 371 of the Penal Code). However, those provisions are more concerned with the public interest in maintaining the functioning of the justice system secret up to a given procedural moment than with the individual right to be presumed innocent (even if the latter does to a certain extent collaterally benefit from the former). That is why, in our view, Article 4 (1) of the Directive cannot be deemed as fully implemented: full implementation would require the enactment of further guarantees.
provisions.textEn: Constitutional provisions concerning rights, freedoms and guarantees are directly applicable and binding on public and private entities.

provisions.comment: See comments to Article 3 of the Directive.

provisions.comment:
As noted in the comment to Article 2 of the Directive, Portuguese criminal procedure normally comprises two pre-trial phases: investigation and inquiry.

At the end of the inquiry the public prosecutor in charge of the case must decide whether or not to prosecute the person, and should prosecute him/her if whenever there is "sufficient evidence" that he/she has committed the crime.

Nevertheless, it is unquestionable in the Portuguese legal system that such a decision whether or not to prosecute is autonomous in relation to the ulterior, hypothetical decision as to whether or not the defendant is indeed guilty of a crime and deserving of a penalty. In this sense, this provision is not detrimental to that contained in the second sentence of Article 4 (1).
provisions.textEn:
(1) Where sufficient evidence has been gathered during the inquiry suggesting that the offence has been committed by the defendant, the Public Prosecution Service shall prosecute the defendant with ten days.

(2) Sufficient evidence is that which reasonably allows for believing that a penalty or a security measure would be imposed on the defendant should he/she face trial.

provisions.comment: The comment to Article 283 CCP, concerning the decision of the public prosecution whether or not to prosecute the defendant at the end of the inquiry phase, applies squarely to the decision of the investigative judge whether or not to indict the person at the end of the instruction phase.
provisions.textEn: If, by the end of the instruction phase, sufficient evidence has been gathered suggesting that the requirements are met for the defendant to be applied a penalty or a security measure later at trial, the judge shall indict the defendant; otherwise, the judge shall rule that the defendant is not to be indicted.

provisions.comment:
As mentioned in a comment to Article 2 of the Directive, the application of pre-trial custodial detention requires, inter alia, "strong evidence" that the defendant has intentionally committed an offence of a certain gravity.

Again, although this provision does to an extent involve an assessment of the possible criminal liability of the person, it is a solid premise in the Portuguese legal system that such an assessment is autonomous in relation to the ulterior, hypothetical decision as to whether or not the defendant is indeed guilty of a crime and deserving of a penalty. In this sense, again, this provision is not detrimental to that contained in the second sentence of Article 4 (1).
provisions.textEn: If other coercive measures are deemed inadequate or insufficient, the judge may subject the defendant to pre-trial custodial detention if: there is strong evidence that the defendant has intentionally committed an offence (...).

items.comment:
Only partially implemented, in terms similar to those expounded in the comments to Article 4 (1) of the Directive.

As stated in that instance, although there are several provisions of ordinary law establishing a duty on public authorities not to make public statements about criminal proceedings in which they intervene, such duties are more concerned with ensuring the (public) interest in the secrecy of justice, than with safeguarding the fundamental (individual) right to be presumed innocent.

Still, such a duty does have a protective side-effect on the right to be presumed innocent, and its breach entails disciplinary (professional) liability by the judge, prosecutor or police officer at issue: see Article 82 of Law no. 21/85 (on judges) and Article 163 of Law no. 47/86 (on public prosecutors); Article 4 of Decree-Law 196/94 (on the Criminal Police [Polícia Judiciária]), Article 4 (1) of Law no. 145/99 (on the National Republican Guard [Guarda Nacional Republicana]), and Article 2 of Law no. 37/2019 (on the Public Security Police [Polícia de Segurança Pública]).

﻿ The Law no. 94/2021, of 21 December, has introduced Article 86 (14), already mentioned above, according to which, if public information provided by the authorities confirm that the person who has been publicly implicated in the case takes on the quality of suspect, then “this person has the right to be heard in the procedure, at his/her request, within a reasonable deadline that should not exceed three months, with the interests of the investigation being secured. Arguably, this provision is still insufficient to secure compliance with Article 4 (2), but it does reinforce to some extent the rights of the person who has been publicly implicated in the case.

items.text: 3. The obligation laid down in paragraph 1 not to refer to suspects or accused persons as being guilty shall not prevent public authorities from publicly disseminating information on the criminal proceedings where strictly necessary for reasons relating to the criminal investigation or to the public interest.

provisions.textEn:
(1) To the exception of the cases where the law provides differently, criminal proceedings are public, or otherwise they will be null.

(2) At the request of the defendant, (...), the judge of instruction, after hearing the Public Prosecutor, may determine that the proceedings be subject to legal secrecy during the inquiry, if he/she believes that their disclosure would affect the rights of procedural subjects or participants; this decision cannot be challenged on appeal.

(3) Where the Public Prosecutor believes that, for the sake of the investigation or of the rights of procedural subjects, proceedings should be secret, he/she may determine that, during the inquiry, the proceedings be subject to legal secrecy. Such a decision must be validated by the judge of instruction within a maximum term of 72 hours.

(...)

(6) Disclosure of proceedings implies (...) the following rights:

(a) The right of the public in general to attend the preliminary hearing and the undertaking of procedural acts at the phase of trial;

(b) The right of the media to report or reproduce procedural acts;

(c) The right to access the file and to obtain copies, extracts, or certified copies of the relevant documents.

(...)

(13) Legal secrecy does not prevent the supply of public information by the judicial authority, when this is necessary for clarifying the truth and does not affect the investigation: (a) At the request of persons who have been publicly implicated in the case, or (b) In order to safeguard the security of persons and assets, or the public order.

provisions.comment: According to Article 87 (2), referred to in Article 88 (3), the judicial decision ordering proceedings to be placed under secrecy of justice should be based on concrete facts or circumstances that enable the assumption that publicity would cause severe damage to the dignity of concerned individuals, to public morals or to the regular undertaking of a procedural act, and it must be revoked as soon as the reasons on which it was based cease to be met.
provisions.textEn:
(1) Within the limits of the law, the media may provide detailed account of the content of procedural acts which are not covered by secrecy of justice or which are open to attendance by the general public.

(2) However, the following is not authorised and may entail committing an offence of disobedience:

(a) The reproduction of procedural documents or of documents somehow incorporated in the proceedings before the sentence of the court of first instance is proffered, unless the documents have been obtained through the request of an official certificate stating the envisaged purpose, or under explicit authorisation by the competent authority presiding over the phase of the criminal procedure ongoing at the time of the publication;

(b) The transmission or recording of images or sound relating to the undertaking of any procedural act, including the trial hearing, unless the judicial authority referred to in the preceding paragraph so allows; however, this authority may not authorise the transmission or recording of images or sound relating to a person against his/her will;

(c) The disclosure by any means of the identity of the victims of a crime of human trafficking, or of a crime against sexual freedom and self-determination, honour or privacy, unless the victim explicitly consents to such a disclosure or the crime is committed through the media.

(3) Until a decision is taken determining the publicity of the hearing, it is prohibited, and it may entail committing an offence of disobedience, to provide an account of procedural acts that have taken place prior to said hearing, if the judge, at his/her own initiative or upon request, has prohibited such an account based on the facts or circumstances mentioned in Article 87 (2).

(4) It is prohibited, and it may entail committing an offence of disobedience, to publish, by any means, conversations or communications intercepted in the course of proceedings, unless they are not subject to secrecy of justice and the parties explicitly consent to their publication.

items.comment:
Only partially implemented.

As expounded below, although defendants, even if detained or imprisoned, normally attend the court as free persons (Article 325 (1) CCP), and although the deployment of coercive methods in order to bring the defendant to court is exceptional (see the provisions and the comments to Article 5 (2) of this Directive), the fact is that no provisions are in place in Portugal which specifically aim at preventing defendants from being "presented as being guilty" in "public".

This leads us to submit that Article 5 (1) of this Directive is not completely implemented into the Portuguese legal system, even if some existing national norms do already accommodate it to a significant extent.

items.text: 2. Paragraph 1 shall not prevent Member States from applying measures of physical restraint that are required for case-specific reasons, relating to security or to the prevention of suspects or accused persons from absconding or from having contact with third persons.

provisions.textEn:
(1) The defendant, even if he/she is detained or imprisoned, attends the trial hearing as a free person, unless cautionary measures are required in order to prevent the risk of him/her escaping or committing acts of violence.

(2) Whenever this is possible, a defendant who is detained or imprisoned is the last person to enter the courtroom and the first person to leave it.

To the exception of the measure provided for in Article 196 [the ‘Statement of Identity and Residence’], no coercive measure may be applied to a defendant if, in the moment of deciding whether or not to apply it, the following requirements are not met:

(a) the defendant has escaped or there is a risk that he/she will escape;

(b) there is a risk that the defendant will disturb the investigation, namely the gathering of evidence or its veracity (by destroying or misrepresenting evidence); or

(c) there is a risk that the defendant will continue his/her criminal activity or severely disturb the public order and peace.

provisions.comment: Summary proceedings are applicable to persons arrested in flagrante delicto for crimes punishable with imprisonment for less than 5 years (or for 5 or more years, but where the public prosecution considers that the offence(s) in question should not be punished with a concrete penalty of imprisonment for over 5 years): see Articles 381 f. CCP.
provisions.textEn:
(1) The detention referred to in the following articles is effected:

(a) In order for the arrested person, within the maximum term of 48 hours, to be brought to trial under summary proceedings or brought before the competent judge for the first judicial interrogation or the application or enforcement of a coercive measure; or

(b) In order for the arrested person to be immediately, or as soon as possible but never after 24 hours, brought before a judicial authority for attending a procedural act.

provisions.comment:
As noted above, the hypothesis contemplated in Article 204 CCP are those where:

- the defendant has escaped or there is a risk that he/she will escape;

- there is a risk that the defendant will disturb the investigation, namely the gathering of evidence or its veracity (by destroying or misrepresenting evidence); or

items.heading: Article 6

items.text: 1. Member States shall ensure that the burden of proof for establishing the guilt of suspects and accused persons is on the prosecution. This shall be without prejudice to any obligation on the judge or the competent court to seek both inculpatory and exculpatory evidence, and to the right of the defence to submit evidence in accordance with the applicable national law.

provisions.comment:
Although this provision (or any other constitutional provision) do not explicitly mention the principle in dubio pro reo, it is undisputed that has constitutional rank, as a concretistion of the principle of presumption of innocence enshrined in the provision.

It should be noted that in dubio pro reo applies only to doubts concerning factual issues. As for doubts concerning legal issues, they are not to be decided according to the interpretation which shows more favourable to the defendant, but rather to the interpretation which the judge deems to be the most accurate (although legal literature does submit that, in some cases, even legal issues should be solved by adopting the most favourable solution to the individual, based on a principle 'in dubio pro libertate'). The non-application or deficient application of the principle in dubio pro reo can be challenged on appeal before the Supreme Court even though its competence is limited legal issues, in that it constitutes a general principle of criminal procedural law (see v.g. the ruling of the Supreme Court of 6 April 1994, process 46092, in www.dgsi.pt, but note that the issue is controversial, as reflected v.g. in the ruling of the Court of Appeal of Lisbon of 23 February 2009, processo 263/2006).
provisions.textEn: Every defendant is presumed innocent until a sentence convicting him/her has become definitive, and must be tried as swiftly as compatible with defence guarantees.

provisions.comment: The accusatorial structure of criminal proceedings means that the prosecuting entity (the public prosecutor) is not the same that takes the decision on the criminal liability of the defendant (the court). Moreover, the Public Prosecution is represented by different magistrates throughout the different stages of the procedure. This separation of functions is evidently relevant to the presumption of innocence, in that it fosters impartiality. On the other hand, Portuguese criminal procedure is not a “procedure of parties”: on the one hand, because the Public Prosecution must abide by a principle of objectivity; on the other hand, because the court has the power to take the measures deemed necessary to ascertain the truth of the facts, irrespective of the contributions of the prosecution and of the defence; finally, because the defence is not burdened with proving the circumstances that may constitute defences.
provisions.textEn: Criminal procedure has accusatorial structure, and the trial hearing and, where required by the law, indictment-related acts abide by the adversarial principle.

provisions.comment: This provision enshrines the so-called 'principle of free assessment of evidence' (princípio da livre apreciação da prova). Again, although this provision does not explicitly state so, the principle in dubio pro reo is clearly embedded in the Portuguese legal system. This provision does however enable the use of so-called “indirect evidence”, whereby from proven facts the court infers – based on logics and/or experience – the verification of other facts. This method has been examined by the Constitutional Court on several occasions and has been ruled not to be unconstitutional (see v.g. the rulings no. 391/2015 and no. 521/2018).
provisions.textEn: Apart from the cases where the law provides otherwise, evidence is assessed according to the rules of experience and the conviction of the competent authority.

(1) At its own initiative or upon request, the court shall order the production of all evidence necessary for ascertaining the truth of the facts and for reaching a proper decision of the case.

(2) If the court finds it necessary to produce evidence which is not contained in the prosecution bill, in the indictment, or in the reply [by the victim] to the indictment, it shall inform the procedural subjects accordingly, as soon as possible, and it shall consign it in writing.

In contrast with in dubio pro reo, the right to remain silent is, however, explicitly provided for in ordinary law, namely in the CCP (see the provisions below).
provisions.textEn: Every defendant is presumed innocent until a sentence convicting him/her has become definitive, and must be tried as swiftly as compatible with defence guarantees.
Any evidence obtained through torture, coercion, infringement of physical or moral integrity or improper intrusion into personal life, domicile, correspondence or telecommunications is null and void.

items.text: 2. Member States shall ensure that suspects and accused persons have the right not to incriminate themselves.
items.comment:
Again, similarly to in dubio pro reo, the principle nemo tenetur se ipsum accusare is not explicitly provided for in Portuguese law, but it is undisputed that it has constitutional rank as a corollary of the principle of presumption of innocence. This understanding has been assertively upheld by the Constitutional Court on numerous occasions, including the rulings no. 695/95, no. 304/2004, no. 181/2005, no. 155/2007 and no. 340/2013. Even recently, in ruling no. 298/2019, the Court held that the documents obtained from a taxpayer during a tax inspection pursuant to his/her general duty to cooperate with tax authorities could not be used as evidence against the same person in an ongoing criminal procedure, based on his/her right not to incriminate him/herself.

Thus, the provisions mentioned above (notably those associated to Article 6 (1) of the Directive) apply here. Nevertheless, it is necessary to note that the CCP does not establish an absolute prohibition of self-incrimination either: it does not impose a ‘patronising' protection of the defendant against him/herself, but rather it admits his/her confession. When questioned at the pre-trial stage, the defendant may confess or deny the facts or his/her participation on the perpetration and refer to any circumstances that may constitute defences, as well as any other that may be relevant to determine his/her responsibility or the applicable sanction (Article 141 (5) CCP); if the defendant confesses the crime in the pre-trial questioning, such a confession will only be read in trial if the requirements mentioned above are met, and, if so, confession will be freely assessed by the judge, as evidence, in trial. In any event, confession alone is insufficient to convict a person, but rather it will only give rise to a conviction if it is made in trial and in compliance with very strict conditions, namely (see Article 344 CCP): if the defendant declares that he/she intends to confess the facts, the judge must ask him/her whether he/she is doing so willingly and free from coercion, and whether he/she is willing to give a full and unreserved confession. Such a confession implies that: (i) the defendant waives production of all evidence, with the consequence that the facts indicated in the bill of prosecution or indictment are established to be proven; (ii) the trial hearing immediately advances to the phase of oral allegations and, should the arguido not be acquitted on other grounds, to the ascertainment of the sanction to be applied; (iii) the court fee is reduced by half. However, this regime will not be applied if: (i) there are other defendants and not all of them give a full, unreserved and consistent confession; (ii) the court suspects that the confession was not authentic or voluntary; or (iii) the offence in question is punishable with imprisonment for over 5 years. Still, if there is a full and unreserved confession, a partial confession or a confession with reservations, the court can decide whether or not, and to what extent, evidence shall be produced.

items.comment:
It is not certain whether it should be deemed fully implemented. As noted, a specific duty impending upon a defendant is to provide the authorities with truthful information about his/her identity and place of residence. This is a peculiar coercive measure which is applied to every defendant due simply to being formally designated as a defendant (arguido). It is called ‘statement of identity and residence’ (termo de identidade e residência) and is regulated in Articles 61 (6) (c) and 196 CCP. The residence provided by the defendant is the one to which all notifications that are to be made to him/her during the course of the procedure will be sent. This coercive measure entails that the defendant be explicitly informed that he/she has a duty not to change residence without reporting such a change to the authorities, that notifications will be sent by regular mail to that address, and that failure on his/her part to comply with such a duty may entail him/her being tried in his/her absence.

At the outset of the phase of trial, the judge notifies the defendant and his/her attorney of the date in which the hearing is to take place, and also designates an alternative date, in case the hearing (as scheduled for the first date) has to be postponed (Article 312 (1) and (2) CCP). This notification is effected through regular mail to the said address (Articles 196 (3) (c) and 113 (1) (c) CCP), and it is not necessary for the defendant to sign a reception form confirming that he/she was indeed notified: the notification is presumed to have been received on the 5th day following that in which it was deposited in the defendant’s mailbox (Article 113 (3) CCP). Such a solution envisages to obviate the cases in which the defendant would refuse to sign the reception form in order to avoid being properly notified. If a defendant who has been duly notified to be present at trial, in the preceding terms, does not attend it at the time appointed for the hearing to commence, the hearing will only be adjourned if the court considers that the presence of the defendant at the beginning of the hearing is absolutely indispensable for ascertaining the truth of the facts (Article 333 (1) CCP). Otherwise, the defendant may be tried in absentia. Thus, the sole condition for a defendant to be tried in absentia is that he/she was notified of the date of the trial by regular mail.

Absence from trial may be justified based on Articles 333 (2) and 117 (2) to (4) CCP, and this will carry the postponement of the hearing, and if the defendant is unable to attend the hearing due. e.g., to his/her age, to a serious illness or to the fact that he/she resides abroad, he/she may request that, or consent to, the hearing being held in his/her absence (Article 333 (4) CCP, which cross-refers to Article 334 (2) CCP). The fact is that Portuguese law does not require the defendant to sign a reception form confirming that the he/she was actually notified of the trial date, which makes it possible that a defendant is unaware that his/her trial is going to take place or even that it has already taken place. This might fall short of the standard envisaged in the Directive, but it does still allow for the assertion that a defendant may only be tried in absentia once he/she “has been informed, in due time, of the trial and of the consequences of non-appearance”. The debate on whether or not the domestic regime complies with the Directive boils down to the interpretation of the expression “has been informed”. If it is construed in the sense that the defendant must get actual knowledge of the date of the trial, then it seems that Portuguese law falls short of the European standard. If, on the contrary, that expression is interpreted in a normative sense (as a sort of implicit presumption), then the Directive can be deemed as implemented, at least in part.

As a matter of fact, the model of notification of the defendant through regular mail, described above, was adopted in reaction to what was perceived as a serious problem of delay in the completion of criminal procedures due to difficulties in notifying defendants, and in our view it is not proscribed by the Directive, but the Directive does require the defendant to be at least given the possibility to rebut the presumption that he/she was informed of the date of the trial and prove that the non-receipt of the notification was not imputable to him/her.

Thus, this provision is fully implemented in the Portuguese legal system.

items.heading: Article 9

transp.label: No national implementation (either officially nor de facto/indirect)

items.comment:
Portuguese legal system does not provide for the right to a new trial as envisaged by Article 9 of the Directive. Portuguese criminal procedure does enable defendants who have been tried in absentia (as any other defendants) to appeal against the decisions convicting them, but it does not enable them to seek a completely “fresh determination of the merits of the case, including examination of new evidence”. Those appeals consist of a review of the decision taken by a court of first instance by a High Court, namely an evaluation of possible mistakes. Such a re-evaluation may focus on legal as well as factual issues (see Article 410 CCP), but by no means does it amount to a retrial. This is patent in the fact that the High Court may only ground its assessment on evidence that has already been produced and hear the recordings of the trial hearing conducted at the court of first instance. The law enables the court of appeal to have the court of first instance ‘renew the evidence’ that has already been produced (Article 430 CCP), but such a possibility is exceptional, and the decision whether or not to order it discretionary. Apart from that, there is an extraordinary type of appeal that does come somewhat close to a fully-fledged re-evaluation of the case – the ‘appeal of review’ (recurso de revisão) regulated in Articles 449 f. of the CCP –, but this type of appeal is not concerned with the case where a person has been tried in absentia, and it is only possible in a very narrow set of circumstances, namely where: (a) another definitive sentence established as false evidence which had been central to the conviction; (b) another definitive sentence deemed proven that a judge or lay-judge committed a crime connected to their function in the process; (c) the facts upon which the conviction is based are irreconcilable with facts which have been proven in another sentence to such an extent as to raise strong doubts on the fairness of the conviction; (d) new facts or evidence are discovered which, either per se or in connection with other which had been appraised in the procedure, raise strong doubts on the fairness of the conviction (note, however, that appeals on this ground are not admissible for the sole purpose of reviewing the quantum of penalty concretely applied: Article 449 (3) of the CCP); (e) it is discovered that evidence which had been central to the conviction was obtained through prohibited methods.

And similar considerations apply to the possibility of ‘resending the file for a new trial’ (reenvio do processo para novo julgamento), regulated in Articles 426 and 426-A CCP. Thus, and to conclude, in order for Portuguese law to comply with the Directive, appeals before the High Courts would, in our view, have to admit significantly wider possibilities to produce new evidence.

provisions.textEn:
(1) Everyone is guaranteed access to the law and to the courts in order to defend the rights and interests conferred upon them by the law, and justice may not be denied to anyone due to the lack of sufficient financial means.

(2) Everyone has the right to legal information and counselling, including the right to be accompanied by an attorney before any public authority.

(4) Everyone involved in judicial litigation has the right to have the case decided within a reasonable term through an equitable process.

(5) Swift proceedings shall be established by the law with a view to ensuring timely protection of fundamental rights, freedoms and guarantees of a personal character.

Any citizen may file a complaint against actions or omissions of public authorities with the Ombudsman, who shall assess them without decision-taking prerogatives and forward to the competent entities and bodies the recommendations that he/she deems necessary to prevent or repair any injustice.
Criminal procedure ensures all guarantees of defence, including the right to appeal.

(1) Courts are the entities that exercise sovereignty with the competence for administering justice in the name of the people.

(2) In administering justice, courts are responsible for ensuring the defence of the citizens’ rights and interests which are protected by the law, for repressing breaches of democratic legality and for solving conflicts of interests, public as well as private.

(...)
Courts are independent and subject only to the law.
In matters submitted to them for judgement, courts may not apply norms which contravene the provisions of the Constitution or the principles enshrined therein.

(1) Court decisions which are not merely administrative in nature [de mero expediente] shall specify the grounds upon which they rely in the legally prescribed form.

(2) Court decisions are binding on all public and private entities and prevail over the decisions of any other authorities.

(3) The law shall regulate the terms under which court decisions are to be executed vis-à-vis any authority, and it shall prescribe the sanctions to be imposed on those who are responsible for any failure to execute them.

(1) In addition to the Constitutional Court, the following categories of court shall exist:

(a) The Supreme Court of Justice and the courts of law of first and second instance;

(b) The Supreme Administrative Court and the remaining administrative and tax courts;

(c) The Court of Auditors.

(2) There may be maritime courts, arbitration courts and courts of peace [julgados de paz].

(3) The law shall specify the cases and forms in which the courts mentioned in the previous paragraphs may separately or conjointly be constituted as conflict-resolution tribunals.

(4) Without detriment to the provisions concerning courts-martial, the existence of courts endowed with exclusive competence for trying certain categories of offences is prohibited.

(1) Every citizen has the right to, either individually or jointly with other citizens, submit petitions, representations, claims or complaints in defence of their rights, of the Constitution, of the law or of general interest to the entities that exercise sovereignty (…) or to any authority, as well as the right to be informed of the result of the consideration thereof within reasonable time.

(3) Everyone is granted the right of popular action [actio popularis], including the right to request that due compensation be given to the aggrieved party or parties, in the cases and under the terms provided for by law, either personally or through associations aimed at defending such interests. This right may be exercised particularly in order to:

(a) Promote the prevention, cessation or judicial prosecution of offences against public health, consumer rights, quality of life and the preservation of the environment, and cultural heritage; (…)

items.comment:
Apart from the rights that have not been implemented into the Portuguese legal system – which inherently have no associated legal remedy –, the breach of the rights provided in the Directive is, in our opinion, subject to “effective remedies”, even though such remedies are not always the same:

(i) If the breach resulted from a judicial decision, then the remedy will generally consist of an appeal before a higher judicial body.

(ii) If the breach resulted from a decision of a criminal police body or a public prosecutor in the context of a criminal procedure, then the remedy may consist either of judicial review by a judge or a complain to the respective hierarchical superior.

(iii) If the breach resulted from another type of action or omission by a public authority, the remedy may consist of initiating a case before an administrative court or of a complaint to the Ombudsman (Provedoria de Justiça).

The following are the implementing provisions, and they are relevant also for the right to an effective remedy enshrined in the other Directives assessed in this report.

items.text: 1. Member States shall ensure that suspects and accused persons have an effective remedy if their rights under this Directive are breached.
items.comment: See the comment and the provisions indicated immediately above in relation to Article 10 of the Directive.

items.text: 2. Without prejudice to national rules and systems on the admissibility of evidence, Member States shall ensure that, in the assessment of statements made by suspects or accused persons or of evidence obtained in breach of the right to remain silent or the right not to incriminate oneself, the rights of the defence and the fairness of the proceedings are respected.
items.comment: Implementation of this provision is secured by the same provisions mentioned above regarding Article 7 of the Directive, on the rights to remain silent and not to incriminate oneself. See also, further above, the comments to Article 3 of the Directive, more specifically regarding Article 32 (2) of the Constitution.
